bindings.claim: Gateway routes POST /links, honoring an Idempotency-Key so retries can't duplicate a link, to the link service, which checks alias availability, inserts the immutable mapping into Links DB, then write-through populates Redis so the first redirect is already a cache hit.

GET /{code} resolves against write-through-populated Redis; on a miss it reads the replica, and only if the replica also misses or is down does it fall back to the primary (rare, safe since rows are immutable) — then fires an acked, retried click event without blocking the 302.

The dashboard query reaches the decoupled Click Counts Store, refreshed every 30s by a 16-way partitioned aggregator fed by an acked, retried click-event enqueue — no click silently dropped, no single consumer bottlenecks at peak.

Hop budget: gateway 5 + service 10 + cache 5 = 20ms on a hit. A miss adds the 5ms failed lookup + replica 15ms = 35ms. The rare triple-miss path adds primary's 10ms for a 45ms worst case — all under the 50ms budget.

A three-tier redirect fallback (cache -> replica -> primary as rare last resort) means no single node failure breaks a redirect; primary is reached only if the replica also misses or is down, and auto re-provisioning rebuilds a fresh standby within minutes of any promotion.

Click events are durably enqueued with broker ack + retry (no silent drop), partitioned across 16 aggregator consumers to survive peak, and batched every 30s with idempotent dedup — monitoring now alerts on queue backlog or aggregator lag before the 5-minute bound is at risk.
Links DB is a single Postgres instance indexed on short code; 20 million rows is well within one instance's capacity with headroom before sharding would ever be needed.

At 2,000 rps average, nearly all reads hit the write-through cache; residual misses go to the replica, primary only a last-resort tier — corrected hop totals (20/35/45ms) hold and no steady load serializes through the primary.

At 10,000 rps peak the cache serves most reads, the replica (sized for 100% of peak) absorbs misses with primary a rare last resort, and 16 parallel aggregator consumers matching the queue's partitions keep counting from backing up.

narrative.overview: This revision closes every gap the panel found. The redirect fallback is now three-tier: cache -> replica -> primary, with primary as a rare last resort, so a newly created link that hasn't replicated yet still redirects instead of 404ing, and no single node — replica included — is a sole in-line dependency. After any promotion, an orchestrator auto-rebuilds a fresh standby from the promoted primary within minutes, so 99.95% doesn't quietly assume only one tolerated failure a month. Corrected hop arithmetic: 20ms on a hit, 35ms on a miss (I'd dropped the 5ms failed lookup), 45ms on the rare triple-miss path touching primary — all under 50ms. The redirect path stays write-free: the service now enqueues click events with broker ack and retry, falling back to a local durable outbox on queue outages, so a click is never silently lost, not just deduped on redelivery. The aggregator runs 16 parallel consumers matching the queue's partitions so 10,000/s peak can't back the pipeline past its 30-second cadence, and monitoring now watches queue backlog and aggregator lag directly. Create is now idempotent on a client-supplied key and checks alias collisions before insert. Links remain insert-only and immutable throughout.

componentRationales.prose: The marketer and the visitor are the same client surface: one issues creates and reads the dashboard, the other just follows redirects. No change requested here.

Unchanged as a thin router carrying a declared 5ms hop budget and emitting metrics, now also honoring an Idempotency-Key on createLink so a client retry after a timeout can't silently duplicate a link.

Still the owner of create and redirect logic, now with an explicit three-tier fallback order (cache, replica, primary) instead of a two-tier chain that relocated the SPOF, plus an idempotency key and alias-collision check on create, and an acked/retried click-event enqueue with a local outbox fallback so a dropped network call can't silently lose a click.
Write-through on create via cachePopulate, unchanged. No TTL needed since mappings never change.

Primary system of record for the immutable mapping, and now also the last-resort read fallback when both cache and replica miss — exceedingly rare, kept safe by immutability, and no longer a node that's simply bypassed by every availability claim while quietly still mattering for writes.

A hot standby streaming from the primary, sized for 100% of peak, that absorbs the overwhelming majority of cache-miss reads. It's now the first fallback tier, not the only one, and after a promotion an orchestrator auto-provisions a fresh standby within minutes so the design doesn't silently tolerate only one failure a month.

A durable, partitioned (16-way), at-least-once log. The service now waits for a broker ack with retry before replying, and falls back to a local durable outbox on a queue outage, so a click event is never silently dropped, only ever deduped on redelivery.

Now explicitly 16 parallel consumers, one per queue partition, auto-scaling to hold the 30-second batch cadence at a sustained 10,000 events/sec peak instead of a single instance that could fall behind exactly when load is highest.
The counter lives here, fully decoupled from the immutable link row, matching the rule that a hot-row counter must not share a row with the entity it's counting.

Now watches queue backlog and aggregator lag directly, in addition to the top-line p99/availability SLOs, so a stalled aggregator or backed-up queue is caught by an alert before the 5-minute freshness bound is actually breached.

criterionNarrations.prose: Create is unchanged in shape — gateway to service to a single immutable insert — but now honors a client idempotency key and checks alias collisions before insert, so a retried submission can't silently duplicate a link, and write-through populates the cache so first-read availability isn't a separate concern.

Redirect is cache-aside with two fallback tiers: replica first, then primary only if the replica also misses or is down. This fixes the false-miss window on a just-created link (replication lag) and removes the replica's status as a sole, unredundant in-line dependency.

The marketer's click count comes from a store built by partitioned batch aggregation off an acked, retried event queue — no click is silently dropped, no consumer bottlenecks at peak, and freshness stays well inside 5 minutes.

Corrected, summed hop budgets — 20ms hit, 35ms single-miss (including the failed cache lookup I'd previously omitted), 45ms rare triple-miss touching primary — all stay under 50ms, replacing the earlier inaccurate 30ms miss-path figure.

A three-tier fallback (cache, replica, primary) plus automated post-promotion re-provisioning means no single node failure, including the replica's, breaks the redirect path, and the design no longer rests on tolerating only one failure per month.

A 30-second aggregation interval with 16 parallel consumers stays well inside the 5-minute bound even at peak, and acked/retried enqueue plus new backlog/lag alerting mean the bound is actually enforced, not just asserted.
20 million indexed rows is a non-issue for a single Postgres primary; this was never threatened by the HA or fallback fixes, which concern failure handling, not volume.

At steady 2,000 rps the cache absorbs nearly all traffic, the replica covers residual misses, and primary is a rare last resort — corrected hop arithmetic confirms this stays well under the latency budget.

At peak 10,000 rps the same cache-plus-replica shape holds with primary as a rare last resort, and because the click pipeline now runs 16 parallel consumers matching the queue's partitions, counting can't fall behind at the exact load that stresses it most.
Links are inserted once via dbWriteCreate and never updated; no edge or operation in the graph performs an update to a link row, consistent with the immutability constraint.
